newsitem.title: GERMANY: Flood-hit Germany sees hope as waters recede.
newsitem.headline: Flood-hit Germany sees hope as waters recede.

text.p: Floods along the River Oder on the border to Poland showed signs of receding on Wednesday after a fresh wave of flooding expected overnight did not happen, officials in east Germany said.
But officials warned that the situation remained critical because the dikes were extremely porous and riddled with weak spots. Efforts would continue to patch them up, they said.

Thousands of soldiers, aid workers and villagers have been sandbagging round the clock since last week in a spectacular effort to prop up sections of water-sodden flood barriers reinforcing the banks of the surging river.

Some of the worst floods this century hit neighbouring Poland and the Czech Republic earlier, claiming 100 lives in the two countries. No deaths have been reported in Germany, but homes, businesses and farms have been extensively damaged.

"We were expecting much worse," said Alwin Ziel, the interior minister of the regional state of Brandenburg, in an interview with Berlin's InfoRadio, referring to a new surge of water feared overnight.
"Water levels could fall considerably by Thursday," another Brandenburg official said, offering a glimmer of hope to the thousands of Germans who live along the river.
But Ziel said that despite dry weather in neighbouring Poland and the Czech Republic where floods have devasted large swathes of farmland, the worst may not yet be over for Germany.

As a precautionary measure, local officials plan mass innoculations this week, fearing that rotting animal carcasses could bring disease to flooded towns south of Frankfurt an der Oder where hundreds of houses were submerged to the rooftops.
But Ziel played down the risk of disease saying that despite the programme there was no real risk and dismissed rumours drinking water was not polluted.
"We have no problems (with polluted water) at present at all and I do not expect such problems in the future," he said.

About 900 soldiers fought overnight to support a critical section of a dike on a 70-km stretch of the border along the Oderbruch plains region where some 5,000 of the 19,000-strong population were evacuated last week.

Oderbruch, once the bread basket of the former communist East Germany, was reclaimed 250 years to create fertile farmland and is vulnerable to flooding because it lies lower than the river and is only protected by a system of dikes.
The last time an Oder dike was breached there was in 1947 near Reitwein where floods devastated homes, crops and claimed lives.
Local officials said that damage to agricultural land had already been greater than they had expected and there were signs the European Union was willing to send aid.

"I think there is a great readiness to help us in Brussels and I have great hopes that we -- particularly in the agricultural sphere -- can expect substantial aid," Brandenburg's farm minister Edwin Zimmermann told InfoRadio.
European Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies is expected to announce European Union aid to German flood victims later on Wednesday.
